passage:
Javier was on his lunch break at the Valencia bike shop when the message arrived: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number has won a new car in the European Mobile Draw. Claim within 2 hours. Pay 190 euros release tax.
His heart jumped. A car. He had cycled to work in the rain for three years. He didn't remember entering anything, but maybe his number had simply been picked. That happened, didn't it?
He sent his sister Nadia a photo of the message with three exclamation marks. Then, because the timer said 1 hour 42 minutes, he paid before she answered.
Nadia called eight minutes later. "Javi. Did you enter a draw?"
"No, but..."
"Then how did you win it?"
He opened his mouth. The payment page had already vanished. The number no longer replied. The car had never existed. Only the 190 euros had been real, and it was gone.

qa.q: How long did the message give Javier to claim the prize?
qa.a: The message said to claim within 2 hours.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling when he read about the car?
qa.a: His heart jumped with excitement, picturing an end to three years of cycling to work in the rain.

qa.q: What could Javier have done before paying?
qa.a: He could have paused to ask what he had entered, waited for Nadia's reply, and checked the sender through an official channel, since a real prize never needs a fee first.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel after the call?
qa.a: Nadia probably feels sorry for Javier and a little frustrated that the timer pushed him to pay before she could answer.

grounding: A young man thrilled by a message saying he won a car he never entered pays a release fee under a countdown, and the fee is all that was real.

passage:
In the hostel mess, Tarun jumped up so fast his dal spilled. "I've won a phone! Latest model!"
The message said his number had been picked in a national lucky draw. Delivery in two days. Just pay 2,999 in tax first, through the link.
The table cheered. Someone started planning a party. Tarun's thumb was already on the link, his heart racing. He had never owned a new phone in his life.
Bhavna, the mess secretary, looked over his shoulder. "Which draw did you enter?"
"I didn't. They picked my number."
"So a stranger is giving you a phone, but you pay them first?"
The cheering faded. Tarun looked at the screen again: a spelling mistake in congratulations, a sender number with twelve digits.
"The fee is the whole trick," Bhavna said. "Real prizes don't charge you."
Tarun sat down slowly, face hot, and deleted the message.

qa.q: How much tax did the message ask Tarun to pay first?
qa.a: It asked him to pay 2,999 in tax first, through the link.

qa.q: Why was Tarun's thumb already on the link?
qa.a: He was thrilled, his heart racing, because he had never owned a new phone, so the excitement rushed him past thinking.

qa.q: Which question from Bhavna broke the spell?
qa.a: Asking which draw he entered, then pointing out that a stranger giving a prize would not make him pay first, helped Tarun notice the warning signs.

qa.q: How might the cheering table feel once the prize turns out to be fake?
qa.a: They may feel a bit sheepish for cheering, and more alert to such messages themselves.

grounding: A student excited by a phone prize he never entered nearly pays a fee until Bhavna asks why a stranger would give him anything.

passage:
Swati, promise you won't laugh. I'm Madhav, and I am officially the biggest idiot in our batch.
So on Monday I get this message: "Congratulations! Your number has won a car in our anniversary lucky draw!" With a photo. A red hatchback. I actually screamed in the hostel corridor.
Did I enter a lucky draw? No. Did I think about that? Also no. I was already imagining driving home to Nagpur.
They said I just had to pay ₹4,999 "registration tax" to release the car. I paid. The next day, ₹12,000 for "insurance." That's when my brain finally woke up. What draw? What company? Why do I pay to win?
I called the number again. Switched off.
My roommate says the fee was the whole trick. There was never any car. The thrill just made me stop thinking for a day.
Anyway. We reported it on the cybercrime portal. Please don't tell the group.

qa.q: How much did Madhav pay as "registration tax"?
How did Madhav feel on getting the message?
qa.a: Madhav felt thrilled and excited, screaming in the corridor, which stopped clear thinking.

qa.q: What should Madhav have asked before paying?
qa.a: Which draw had actually been entered, whether the company was real, and why paying was needed to receive a prize.

qa.q: How does Madhav's roommate see the scam?
qa.a: The roommate sees the fee itself as the whole trick, since there was never any car.

grounding: A young adult describes winning a prize never entered, the thrill cutting short all thinking, and paying the fee that was the actual theft.

passage:
Monday. A message popped up on Anirban's phone: "You have won the latest smartphone in our festive draw! Claim within 48 hours." Anirban grinned all through his lecture. His old phone's screen had been cracked for months.
Tuesday. The "prize desk" called. Friendly voice. Only a small ₹1,500 delivery tax, then the phone would ship. Anirban paid through the link right away. He felt lucky, chosen, for once.
Thursday. Another call. Customs had held the parcel. ₹6,000 more. Anirban hesitated.
His roommate Harish looked over his shoulder. "Which draw did you enter?"
Anirban opened his mouth. He hadn't entered any draw.
"And why would a prize need tax before delivery?" Harish asked quietly.
Anirban's excitement drained away. He felt stupid and angry at once. That evening they blocked the number and reported it on the cybercrime portal together.

qa.q: How much did Anirban pay as delivery tax?
qa.a: ₹1,500 delivery tax.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when he first saw the message?
qa.a: Anirban felt excited and lucky, grinning through his lecture because his old phone was cracked.

qa.q: What questions helped Anirban see the scam?
qa.a: Harish asked which draw he had entered and why a prize would need tax before delivery.

qa.q: How did Harish respond to Anirban's situation?
qa.a: Harish questioned gently rather than mocking, and helped block and report the number.

grounding: It shows a young adult thrilled by a prize never entered, paying a fee, then seeing through the scam when asked what he entered.

passage:
Chinmay, you want to know why your Rukmini Aaji tears up every letter that says "Congratulations"? Sit.
When I was twenty, just married, a letter came to our house in Pune. Printed on thick paper with a gold stamp. "You have won ₹1 lakh in the International Lucky Draw." In those days, ₹1 lakh was a house.
I danced in the kitchen. I didn't ask myself which lucky draw I had entered. I hadn't entered anything.
The letter said to send ₹500 by money order for "processing tax." I took it from my savings tin and sent it that very day. Then another letter asked for ₹1,000. And another.
It was your Aajoba who finally asked, "Why must you pay to receive a gift?" I had no answer.
There was never any lakh. Only my ₹500 and my pride, gone. Since then, when luck asks for money first, I know it isn't luck.

qa.q: How much did young Rukmini send by money order first?
qa.a: ₹500 by money order.

qa.q: How did young Rukmini feel when the letter arrived?
qa.a: Young Rukmini felt overjoyed, dancing in the kitchen, which stopped any question about whether anything had been entered.

qa.q: What turning point in the story revealed the scam?
qa.a: Her husband asked why she must pay to receive a gift, and she had no answer.

qa.q: How might young Rukmini's husband have felt seeing the letters?
qa.a: Rukmini's husband was probably worried and puzzled, questioning why a real prize would need money first.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a lottery she never entered, the thrill making her pay a fee that was the actual theft.

passage: Sudha was on the crowded local train to college, squeezed against the door, when the message arrived: "Congratulations! Your number has won a new car in our anniversary lucky draw. Pay a small processing tax within 30 minutes to claim." A photo of a shiny red hatchback. Her heart thumped. A car! She pictured driving Mummy to the temple, the look on her cousins' faces. The message said 27 minutes left. The train lurched and the network kept dropping. She started opening her payment app, hands sweaty. Then Avni, her classmate, squashed beside her, glanced at the screen. "Which draw did you enter?" Sudha opened her mouth. She hadn't entered anything. She had never even heard of the shop. The thrill drained out of her so fast she felt dizzy. "If it's real, why would I pay them?" she said slowly. Avni nodded. At the next station Sudha blocked the number and reported the message.

qa.q: What did the message say Sudha had won?
qa.a: A new car in an anniversary lucky draw.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when she first read the message?
qa.a: Sudha felt thrilled and excited, her heart thumping as she pictured driving Mummy to the temple.

qa.q: What question broke the spell, and what did Sudha do next?
qa.a: Avni asked which draw Sudha had entered; seeing she had entered none, Sudha realised the fee was the real theft, then blocked and reported the number.

qa.q: How did Avni help without embarrassing Sudha?
qa.a: Avni asked one simple, curious question instead of mocking, letting Sudha reach the answer herself.

grounding: Shows a person told they have won a car in a draw they never entered and asked for a fee, with the thrill and a countdown cutting thinking short.
